conversation.content:
Hello—thank you for making time to talk today. My name is Dr. Bennett, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. First, congratulations on your new baby; I know these early weeks can feel like a whirlwind of joy, worry, and exhaustion all at once.

I’d like to check in on how you’re feeling emotionally by using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply 10 questions that help us spot signs of depression or anxiety that sometimes creep up after childbirth. Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the medical team that looks after you. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll go at your pace.

I’ll ask each question about how you’ve felt in the past seven days, and you can answer however feels most true for you. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, when you were able to sleep, did you still wake up feeling happy and able to look forward to the day, or did you find that hard to do?
I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—most nights I get a decent stretch—so when I wake up I feel okay, not bouncing-off-the-walls happy, but I can look forward to the day.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—like when my husband tried to swaddle the baby and it looked more like a burrito roll gone wrong. It’s not constant giggles, but I can see the funny side most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve still looked forward to little things—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller when it’s sunny. It’s not huge excitement, but I do find myself thinking, “Oh, that’ll be nice,” and meaning it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her, I might think, “Maybe I jostled her too much,” but it passes in a second. I don’t sit there beating myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different, even though she looks perfectly fine. It’s quick—like a flash—and then I’m okay again. It’s not all day, just little moments.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any sudden panic or that shaky, heart-racing feeling. I might feel a brief flutter of worry, but it never turns into real fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when the baby wouldn’t settle and the laundry was piling up, I felt a bit swamped. It passed once she finally napped and I could fold a basket. It’s not constant, just now and then.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleeping’s actually fine. I’m tired from night feeds, but once I’m out, I stay asleep. I don’t lie there feeling unhappy or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get a little tired or overwhelmed sometimes, but I haven’t felt truly sad or down. Most moments feel pretty steady—just normal new-mom stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had any of those tearful spells. I might feel a bit weepy when I’m really tired, but it’s rare and passes quickly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Patient-endorsed symptoms  
- Mild, transient worries (“flash” concerns about infant breathing)  
- Occasional feeling of being overwhelmed when tasks accumulate; resolves with situational change (baby naps, chores completed)  

Absence of high-risk indicators  
- No persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, crying spells, panic attacks, sleep-onset or maintenance problems linked to mood, or self-harm ideation  

Pattern  
Overall affective state described as “steady,” with preserved capacity for enjoyment and humor; distress is situational and self-limited. No red-flag signs for major postpartum depression or anxiety on this screen.
